---
title: "Figures"
engine: pari-gp
---

gp has no notion of a "current figure" the way R or matplotlib do. A plot
reaches the document because you asked gp for it: `plothexport("svg", ...)`
returns the SVG document itself, and the engine turns any cell whose output is
an SVG into a figure.

## A first plot

```{gp}
#| fig-cap: "sin(x) on [-3, 3]"
#| fig-alt: "A sine wave with two full oscillations"
plothexport("svg", X = -3, 3, sin(X))
```

`print(plothexport(...))` works too; both the quoted value gp prints for a
string and the raw printed form are recognised.

## Cross-references

Give the cell a `label` starting with `fig-` and the figure becomes
cross-referenceable, as in @fig-zeta.

````markdown
```{gp}
#| label: fig-zeta
#| fig-cap: "Real part of zeta on the critical line"
plothexport("svg", T = 0, 50, real(zeta(1/2 + I*T)))
```
````

```{gp}
#| label: fig-zeta
#| fig-cap: "Real part of zeta on the critical line"
#| fig-alt: "An oscillating curve crossing zero several times"
plothexport("svg", T = 0, 50, real(zeta(1/2 + I*T)))
```

## Several curves at once

`plothexport` takes a vector of expressions, and the flag `1` joins the points:

```{gp}
#| label: fig-bessel
#| fig-cap: "Bessel functions $J_0$ and $J_1$"
#| fig-alt: "Two damped oscillating curves"
plothexport("svg", X = 0.1, 20, [besseljh(0, X), besseljh(1, X)], 1)
```

## Size

`fig-width` sets the CSS width of an inline SVG; gp's own width and height go
to `plothsizes`-aware functions, or as the last arguments of `plothexport`.

```{gp}
#| fig-width: 60%
#| fig-cap: "The same curve at 60% width"
plothexport("svg", X = -3, 3, cos(X))
```

## How it is emitted

For HTML the SVG goes **straight into the page**, so it stays sharp at any zoom
and there is no file to keep track of. For every other format the SVG is
written to the document's `_files` directory and referenced as an image, which
Quarto copies and cleans up as usual.

## Which plotting functions work

The rule is simple: **a cell whose output is an SVG document becomes a
figure**. Every gp function that returns SVG therefore works, and there are
three of them:

| Function | Draws |
| --- | --- |
| `plothexport("svg", X = a, b, expr)` | a function of one variable |
| `plothrawexport("svg", xs, ys)` | a list of points you computed yourself |
| `plotexport("svg", w)` | a drawing built with `plotinit` / `plotrecth` |

`plothrawexport` is how you plot data rather than a formula:

```{gp}
#| label: fig-raw
#| fig-cap: "The first 40 values of $\\pi(n)$"
#| fig-alt: "A rising step-like sequence of points"
xs = vector(40, n, n);
ys = vector(40, n, primepi(n));
plothrawexport("svg", xs, ys)
```

And `plotexport` draws a rectangle you composed yourself:

```{gp}
#| label: fig-rect
#| fig-cap: "A drawing composed with plotinit and plotrecth"
#| fig-alt: "A smooth oscillating curve"
plotinit(0, 480, 300);
plotrecth(0, X = 0, 10, sin(X) * exp(-X/5));
plotexport("svg", 0)
```

## What does not work

`ploth`, `plothraw` and `plotdraw` draw to a screen device, so there is nothing
for the engine to capture during a render — use their `…export` counterparts
above.

`psploth` and `psplothraw` write a PostScript file (`pari.ps` by default)
rather than returning a string. No browser renders PostScript, so the engine
does not pick these up. If you need PostScript, call them, convert the file
yourself, and reference the result with ordinary markdown.
